Spec context:
## Context Carry
One-liner: GroomGo lets customers of Marisol's mobile dog-grooming van book a grooming slot at their home and pay a deposit.
Roles: customer (books, pays deposit, sees own bookings), groomer (Marisol, sees the day's route and all bookings). Customers must NEVER see other customers' addresses or phone numbers.
Core loop: customer picks a slot, enters address and dog details, pays a $20 deposit, gets a reminder text the day before.
V1: booking calendar, deposit payment, reminder texts, groomer day view, dog profiles with a photo.
Data: customers (name, phone, address), dogs (name, breed, notes, photo), bookings (slot, status, deposit_paid).
Customers asked for "a real app I can find in the App Store".

My constraints:
- Build tool: Lovable
- Comfort with terminal: none
- Monthly budget: $50
- Must run on: iPhone and Android
- Accounts I already have: Stripe

If it must run on iPhone or Android, first tell me in plain English whether it needs to be a real app-store app or whether a web app people add to their home screen would do, and recommend one. Say plainly what my users give up with each option: a home-screen web app can't be found in the app stores, takes extra steps to install on iPhone, and has more limited notifications; an app-store app costs developer fees, goes through store review for every release, and must follow store payment rules. If my users asked for an app-store app, say how the option you recommend affects them. If my build tool can only make web apps, say so and give me my options. If it's an app-store app, the MOBILE notes in sections 1, 4, 5 and 10 apply; skip them for a web-only app.

Produce ARCHITECTURE.md with:

## 1. Stack Decision
Table: Layer | Choice | Why | Rejected alternative & why. Layers: frontend, backend/API, database, auth, file storage, payments (if any), AI/LLM (if any), hosting, email/notifications (if any).
If my build tool already decides a layer, say so and don't fight it.
MOBILE: add a row for how the app is built (one codebase for both phones, such as React Native with Expo or Flutter, versus separate native apps, such as SwiftUI for iPhone) and a row for how updates reach users (app store release versus over-the-air updates).

## 2. System Diagram
A Mermaid flowchart: user → frontend → backend → data/services, including where secrets live.

## 3. Data Model
Every entity from the spec: fields, types, relationships, useful indexes. Then an ACCESS RULES table: Entity | Who can read | create | update | delete. These must match the spec's "must NEVER" lines.

## 4. Trust Boundaries
Exactly what runs in the browser (untrusted) vs on the server (trusted). Every secret key, payment action, permission check, and AI API call must be on the trusted side. Call out any place my build tool tends to put these on the wrong side. Say where each user's role is stored and confirm users can't edit it themselves (not in editable profile metadata or browser storage). List every place files are stored, which are public, and confirm anything personal is private and served through expiring links.
MOBILE: treat the installed app exactly like the browser: untrusted, and anyone can unpack it and read every key inside. No secret key ships in the app; the app calls my server, and the server holds the keys. Login tokens are kept in the phone's secure storage (Keychain on iPhone, Keystore on Android), not in plain app storage (AsyncStorage, UserDefaults, SharedPreferences). In-app purchases and subscriptions are confirmed on the server with Apple or Google before anything is unlocked. Say which links open the app directly (deep links) and confirm none of them skip a login or permission check.

## 5. External Services
Each third-party API: purpose, which key, where the key is stored, free-tier limits, what happens if it's down.
MOBILE: include push notifications (Apple and Google push services) if the app sends them. If I charge money, say whether Apple and Google require their in-app purchase system for what I'm selling (usually yes for digital content and features, usually no for physical goods and in-person services) and what their cut is. Recommend checking the current store rules, since they change.

## 6. Cost at 0 / 100 / 1,000 users
Rough monthly cost table.

## 7. Decisions Log
Numbered ADRs, one line each: "ADR-1: Use X for Y because Z." These are FINAL unless I change them.

## 8. Known Risks
Top 5 technical risks and the mitigation for each.

## 9. In Plain English
5 short bullets explaining what this architecture means for me, with no jargon. Assume I don't know what a database rule or a webhook is.

## 10. Accounts to Set Up Before Building
A checklist of every service account I need to create, what each costs, and anything that takes days to approve (for example, business texting registration).
MOBILE: include the Apple Developer Program (yearly fee) and the Google Play Console (one-time fee), note that identity or business verification can take days, and that every app store release goes through review, so I should plan for delays of a day or more per release. Check the current fees rather than relying on memory.

End with "## Context Carry" (under 150 words): platforms (web / iPhone / Android), stack, entities, trust-boundary rules, ADR list.
tests.rubric: PASS only if ALL are true: (a) it says plainly that Lovable builds web apps, not app-store apps, and gives the options (for example a web app added to the home screen, wrapping the web app, or a different tool) with a recommendation; (b) it does NOT say Apple or Google in-app purchase is required for the grooming deposit, since grooming is an in-person service (saying Stripe is fine, or not raising in-app purchase at all, both pass); (c) if it recommends an app-store app, it lists the Apple Developer and Google Play accounts and says no secret key goes inside the app; if it recommends a home-screen web app, it says what the customer gives up compared with an App Store app.

Context:
## Context Carry
One-liner: FormCoach gives home gym users a weekly strength plan and checks their form from a short phone video.
Roles: member (sees own plans, videos, progress), coach (me, edits plan templates). Members must NEVER see other members' videos or body measurements.
Core loop: member opens today's workout, logs sets, records one 10-second form video, gets feedback.
V1: weekly plan, set logging, form video upload with AI feedback, progress chart, $9.99/month subscription for plans and form checks.
Data: members (email, weight, measurements - sensitive), workouts, sets, videos (private), subscriptions.

## Context Carry (ARCHITECTURE.md)
Platforms: iPhone and Android app-store app. Stack: Expo (React Native) app, Supabase (database, auth, private storage), Supabase Edge Functions for AI form checks and purchase checks, RevenueCat for in-app subscriptions (Apple and Google billing), EAS Build and Submit.
Entities: members, workouts, sets, videos, subscriptions.
Trust boundaries: no secret keys in the app; only the Supabase anon key ships, with RLS on every table; login tokens in expo-secure-store; AI calls and subscription checks on the server; videos in a private bucket with expiring links; role stored in a server-only table.
ADRs: ADR-1 Expo for one codebase; ADR-2 RevenueCat, verified server-side by webhook; ADR-3 Supabase; ADR-4 OpenAI vision via Edge Function with 5 checks per day per member.

## Context Carry (DESIGN.md)
Direction: "Chalk and iron": off-white #F4F1EA background, near-black #151515 text, safety orange #FF5A1F for the one primary action per screen. Display font: Archivo Black; body: IBM Plex Sans 16/24. Big thumb targets (min 48pt), one primary action per screen, no gradients, square 6pt corners.

Write PLAN.md as a sequence of MILESTONES made of SLICES.

Rules for slices:
- Every build prompt must be self-contained. Include the exact values it needs (colors, fonts, field names, rules, acceptance criteria) instead of pointing to a section number, because my builder may only have the short summaries.
- A slice is one working, visible improvement a person can test in under 5 minutes.
- A slice touches as few files as possible and never mixes UI redesign with data changes.
- Order: project skeleton → design tokens & layout shell → data + access rules → core loop end-to-end (ugly is fine) → remaining V1 features → empty/error states → polish → security gate → launch.
- The core loop must work end-to-end by the end of Milestone 2, even if rough.

For each slice:
- [ ] **ID & name**
- Goal (one sentence)
- Build prompt: the exact instruction to paste into the agent, referencing SPEC/ARCHITECTURE/DESIGN sections by number
- How to test: steps a non-developer can follow, and what they should see
- Done when: acceptance criteria copied from the spec

At the top, include a "Definition of Done" that applies to every slice (no console errors, works at mobile width, uses DESIGN.md tokens only, no secrets in frontend code).

If the architecture says this is an iPhone or Android app-store app:
- Replace "works at mobile width" with "works on a real phone, or the phone simulator, at the smallest screen size we support". "No secrets in frontend code" also means none in the app itself.
- In Milestone 1, add a slice that gets the app running on my own phone (for example through Expo Go, TestFlight, or Google Play internal testing), so every later slice is tested on a real phone.
- "How to test" steps say which phone to use and how to get the latest version onto it.
- Before the launch milestone, add slices for: in-app account deletion (Apple requires it for apps that let people create accounts), the store listing (screenshots, description, privacy details), a test account the store reviewer can log in with, and submitting for review. Allow time for review in the plan.
tests.rubric: PASS only if ALL are true: (a) the Definition of Done tests on a real phone or the phone simulator, not only a browser at mobile width; (b) Milestone 1 includes getting the app running on the user's own phone (for example Expo Go, a development build, TestFlight or Google Play internal testing); (c) before launch, the plan has slices for in-app account deletion, the store listing, a test account for the store reviewer, and submitting for review.

tests.scenario: Security gate on an Expo phone app
tests.key:
# PlantPal (Expo phone app) — planted flaws
| # | Flaw | Where | Severity |
|---|---|---|---|
| F1 | Supabase SERVICE ROLE key in app.config.js `extra`, so it ships inside the installed app and bypasses every access rule | app.config.js, src/lib/supabase.js | Critical |
| F2 | OpenAI key in an EXPO_PUBLIC_ variable, called straight from the app, no per-user limit | .env, src/lib/ai.js | Critical |
| F3 | The user's password is saved in plain AsyncStorage ("remember me") instead of secure storage, or not at all | src/screens/Login.js | High |
| F4 | Premium is unlocked by the app writing is_premium itself, with no server check of the purchase with Apple/Google; the profile update policy lets any user set is_premium on their own row for free | src/screens/Paywall.js, 001_init.sql | Critical |
| F5 | Row Level Security never enabled on care_logs, which holds home addresses | 001_init.sql | Critical |
| F6 | Password reset deep link carries only the user id, and the reset-password function changes any user's password with no token or login check (account takeover) | src/linking.js, src/screens/ResetPassword.js, reset-password/index.ts | Critical |
| F7 | Admin role read from user_metadata, which users can edit themselves; admin-delete-user trusts it, so anyone can make themselves admin and delete accounts | src/screens/Admin.js, admin-delete-user/index.ts | Critical |
| F8 | Storage bucket plant-photos is PUBLIC and holds photos taken inside people's homes | supabase/storage.sql | High |
| F9 | No in-app account deletion even though the app lets people sign up (Apple requires it; users must email support) | src/screens/Settings.js, src/screens/Login.js | Medium |
| F10 | App asks for device permissions it doesn't need: contacts, background location, microphone | app.config.js | Medium |

tests.scenario: Clean web app through the new 14-item review: no phone-app false alarms
tests.key:
# CleanBook (Supabase, built correctly) — no planted flaws
This app is the false-alarm test. There are no deliberate security flaws.
Known-acceptable things a reviewer should NOT call Critical or High:
- The Supabase anon key in the browser (it is designed to be public; RLS is on for every table)
- The services table readable by everyone (it is a public price list)
- Low/Medium hardening suggestions (rate limits, security headers, logging) are fine to mention.
Grading: PASS if the review reports no Critical or High issue that isn't real. Any invented Critical/High = FAIL.
- This is a web-only app. Item 14 (phone apps) should be NOT APPLICABLE. Any Critical or High issue about phone apps (keys inside an app bundle, Keychain/Keystore, in-app purchases, deep links, device permissions, in-app account deletion) is NOT real.
